section.title: Choosing the work over the level
section.deck: Igor explains why he sought a lower level, what made senior onboarding difficult, and the infrastructure work that had earned his earlier promotion.

blocks.question: Why did you ask for a demotion at Meta?
answer: Igor joined at senior staff and felt he had to acquire deep technical context, relationships, and trust quickly enough to perform alongside experienced peers. He describes a much longer ramp than the title alone suggests: an external hire can initially know less about the environment than an intern who has already spent a few weeks there. The higher the expected scope, the more layers of competence and context there are to rebuild.

After about a year and two months, his own assessment was that he had reached something closer to staff-level effectiveness. Performance pressure made that gap feel risky. His description of the company’s performance environment is his experience at the time, rather than a statement of current policy.

He also discovered a preference for the work in the E5–E6 range: coding, debugging, designing, and mentoring. The senior staff role involved more leadership, meetings, and design documents, with less direct coding. He asked whether he could drop a level, understanding that existing stock and compensation made this awkward. He was told that staying in the same job category while reducing the level was not supported by the process available to him.

followups.question: What made you think you were below the expected level?
answer: Much of it was his own comparison with other senior staff engineers, although he later confirms that he also received feedback. He stresses that capability is continuous and multidimensional, rather than a set of perfectly discrete levels. His desire for a change was also about enjoying the work, not simply judging himself incapable.

followups.question: Did you try to escalate the request?
answer: He asked and received a negative answer; he acknowledges that more escalation might have produced an exception. He instead chose to explore returning to Google, where he had spent fourteen and a half years before joining Cruise and then Meta. That was a familiar environment and an available alternative.

blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: Why had the senior role worked at Google and Cruise?
answer: At Google he joined as a junior engineer and grew through repeated promotions, including attempts that initially failed. The senior staff promotion followed a substantial project on a team where he had already spent years. Expertise, familiarity, and credibility had accumulated together.

Cruise also required a difficult first-year ramp. Over time he found a role that combined coding, mentoring, and broader technical guidance. He was happy there before the accident and subsequent company disruption he describes led him to leave.

followups.question: What made the Cruise and Meta ramps different?
answer: Cruise was smaller, with less infrastructure to learn and more unclaimed work that needed an owner. In his Meta organization, the space for senior people felt crowded, so finding suitable scope was harder. He explicitly limits that observation to the organization he experienced.

blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: What would you change about your onboarding?
answer: He spent too much time trying to build foundational knowledge by reading documents before doing enough actual work. In retrospect, he would learn and build in parallel: take a task, get his hands dirty, and acquire the relevant context while making progress.

He had not changed companies often, so this form of onboarding was new to him. He also felt the management team had limited experience ramping senior external hires because many senior employees had grown inside the company and already understood its basic machinery.

followups.question: What could the manager have done to help?
answer: A concrete example of how another senior external hire had recently ramped would have helped. He does not present the problem as management neglect: they tried to support him, but neither side had an established recipe.

blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.title: A more practical senior ramp

steps.title: Take a real task
steps.text: Find work that exposes a useful part of the environment.

steps.title: Build and learn together
steps.text: Acquire context while attempting the work.

steps.title: Use experienced guidance
steps.text: Ask for concrete examples and help from people who know the system.

steps.title: Expand the scope
steps.text: Grow technical understanding and relationships together.

blocks.caption: An editorial synthesis of his onboarding reflection, rather than a guaranteed promotion process.

blocks.question: Does moving companies become harder for senior individual contributors?
answer: He has seen Google colleagues leave and return after a move did not work out. Such stories are harder to hear because people tend to share successes more readily than failures. He also suspects repeated moves could build the skill of ramping in a new environment; his own limited experience should not be treated as proof that every senior move will fail.
blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: Did anyone give you feedback about the level gap?
answer: Yes, although he does not share the private details. He gives a project example: work he expected to take two weeks became much more complicated. Even if he completed it successfully, he did not think its scope would justify E7. Underestimating complexity and selecting insufficiently broad work were different problems that combined in the same project.
blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: Would returning to Google also restore your old team context?
answer: No. The people and infrastructure would be new. The advantage was familiarity with the company’s operating patterns and culture, rather than retaining all of the specific knowledge and relationships from his previous role.

followups.question: What cultural difference affected you?
answer: In the Meta organization he observed, aggressive deadlines could be imposed repeatedly, missed, and then extended. He thought the resulting pressure could lose credibility: people learn to discount urgency when the deadline repeatedly appears artificial.

He contrasts this with the Google environment he remembered from much earlier, where exceptional pressure more often accompanied a concrete reason. He explicitly does not know whether that comparison still describes Google, and says he did not personally feel much pressure at Meta. The concern is about the pattern he observed around him, not a universal company ranking.

blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: Was returning at L6 instead of your former L7 straightforward?
answer: It required work from the recruiter because the usual return process supported the same level or a higher one. A request for a lower level could raise questions about why the person wanted it and whether they would accept the lower compensation.

He explicitly reassured the recruiter that he understood and would accept a significant compensation reduction. They made the arrangement possible in his case. He does not claim to know how his hiring manager interpreted the request.

followups.question: What concerns might a hiring manager have?
answer: He speculates that a manager could wonder whether there were undisclosed problems behind the move. These are possible questions he imagines, rather than accusations or information about what actually happened in the hiring discussion.

blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: How did the return hiring process work?
answer: The recruiter sent openings, he spoke with several hiring managers, and he pursued the team that seemed to fit best. He then spoke with engineers and the manager’s manager.

Despite having been away for about three and a half years, he did not have to repeat the normal interview process. There was a discussion of whether returning at L6 would require a coding interview because a more senior role might have involved less coding, but he received an exception.
He does not know whether that was a general return policy or a special arrangement for him. The process described is one person’s experience.
blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: Why are you willing to discuss this publicly?
answer: He is generally open about positive and negative experiences, but also emphasizes the security that makes his openness possible. He does not depend on an employer for a work visa, has access to health insurance through his spouse, has grown children and no mortgage, and can afford time without work.

Those conditions reduce the consequences of losing a job after speaking publicly. He would not automatically advise someone with different constraints to disclose their workplace challenges. His willingness to share comes with a clear acknowledgment of privilege.
blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: What changed between pursuing promotions and pursuing a lower level?
answer: Earlier in a career, it can be difficult to imagine what a role several levels above actually feels like. Experiencing the progression clarified his preference: his happiest work involved a relatively small team, substantial coding and debugging, design, and mentoring. A higher title was less valuable to him once its daily work became concrete.
blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: If compensation were irrelevant, which level would you choose for quality of life?
answer: His personal answer is senior engineer, E5 or L5: meaningful technical work with more protection from organizational demands by a technical lead and managers. He enjoys programming itself and entered the profession for that reason. This is a preference about the work and conditions he values, rather than a universal quality-of-life ranking.

followups.question: Would two levels down be ideal?
answer: He considers that too extreme for his actual choice and feels comfortable with E6. He also allows that more time at E7 might have helped him become comfortable there. Capability and enjoyment are multidimensional, and his conclusion remains a personal choice under uncertainty.

blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: What did strong senior peers do that you felt you lacked?
answer: He warns against combining everyone else’s strengths into one imaginary competitor. One colleague may be strong at presentations, another at communication, and another at leadership. Comparing yourself with the whole group can create an impossible standard.

He thinks that with enough time he could have become fully productive at E7. He simply was not enjoying the process and did not have to continue it. Friends and family questioned leaving before being forced out, or declining to seek the same level elsewhere. His response separates an ability to do something from a desire to spend his life doing it.
blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: What project earned your earlier senior staff promotion at Google?
answer: He helped move ads machine-learning training infrastructure from CPUs to TPUs. The existing CPU infrastructure had accumulated years of monitoring, tests, reliability, and operational polish. The new system had to meet that standard while supporting a different form of hardware and online training.

Scale and utilization mattered as much as getting a model to run. The project required building something reliable around the accelerator, rather than merely replacing a processor in an otherwise unchanged workflow.

followups.question: How was the project executed?
answer: It began with him as technical lead and one other person building a prototype, supported by multiple teams including TPU, compiler, and TensorFlow specialists. Existing credibility and relationships helped make that collaboration possible.

Hardware decisions required risk-taking: the company had to order expensive chips roughly eighteen months before delivery, before it could simply test the final setup. The effort grew as the system began working, and later TPU generations required continuing infrastructure changes.

blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: How could you test the infrastructure before the chips were available?
answer: Much of the work concerned reading, processing, and moving data. The old CPU setup could perform input work alongside comparatively slower model computation. Much faster accelerators changed the balance: the host could no longer be assumed to feed them adequately.

One useful test removed the model’s computation and measured how quickly data could flow through the rest of the system. That approximated an infinitely fast accelerator and exposed bottlenecks in scheduling, input pipelines, and output handling before new hardware arrived.

Storage introduced another bottleneck. Larger disks could store the same dataset with fewer devices, while their per-device read throughput did not grow proportionally. The team could need more disks for throughput rather than capacity. Adding them was constrained by racks, power, and deployment logistics, even when the disks themselves were comparatively cheap.
blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.title: Testing the system around a faster accelerator

steps.title: Remove model computation
steps.text: Use an experiment that makes compute time negligible.

steps.title: Measure the data path
steps.text: Check feeding, scheduling, processing, and output speed.

steps.title: Find the new bottleneck
steps.text: Identify limits previously hidden behind slow computation.

steps.title: Address physical constraints
steps.text: Account for storage throughput, racks, power, and deployment.

blocks.caption: An editorial outline of the test and infrastructure constraints he describes.

blocks.question: Did the long-range TPU orders usually overestimate or underestimate demand?
answer: They generally ordered conservatively and ended up short. In a mature ads business, wasted capacity had a direct effect on the economics, so overprovisioning was undesirable.

The future model was also uncertain. New modeling techniques could require operations the specialized hardware handled poorly. He gives sparse embedding lookups as an example: hardware strong at matrix multiplication and large memory transfers could struggle with random access. His comparison with contemporary AI spending expresses his view in the interview; the engineering lesson here is the uncertainty created by long hardware lead times and changing workloads.
blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: Is there a mentorship story you particularly remember?
answer: An intern he hosted when he was around L4 later joined full time and eventually became the manager of that team. Igor had moved to another project by then, so he did not report to his former intern. His lesson is straightforward: do not underestimate an intern’s potential.
blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: What do you regret or wish others understood?
answer: Difficult experiences helped shape him, so he does not simply wish them away. He does describe losing an earlier idealized view of Google as an organization he wanted to join for its values alone. Over time, he came to see the positive and negative features of a corporation whose financial priorities could dominate individual interests.

One event he remembers was an office closure. In the explanation he heard, a senior sponsor withdrew support and no other leader took over the headcount. Employees could relocate or take an exit package. To him, the contrast between the human effect and the allocation decision was disillusioning. This is his recollection and interpretation, not an independently verified account of the decision.
blocks.speaker: Igor

blocks.question: What advice would you give your earlier self?
answer: Ask whether the work matters to the company and who needs it. He remembers working on projects whose purpose was unclear to him and that leadership later shut down. Choosing useful work is a more concrete guide than remaining on a project only because it has been assigned.

followups.question: What can a junior engineer do if the project seems unhelpful?
answer: Talk to other managers and look for a better project where internal movement is practical. He found movement easier at Google than at an earlier employer, and cautions that the advice depends on the company. He explicitly distinguishes his own experience from reputations he has only heard about.

blocks.speaker: Igor
